eponyms.name: the Earl of Sandwich
eponyms.origin: Named after the Earl of Sandwich, its supposed inventor. The naming is well recorded; the story of exactly how he came to eat it is less certain.

eponyms.name: Charles Boycott
eponyms.origin: From Charles Boycott, an English land agent in Ireland who, in 1880, was shunned in a campaign organized by the Irish Land League after evicting tenants.

eponyms.name: James Brudenell, 7th Earl of Cardigan
eponyms.origin: Named after James Brudenell, the 7th Earl of Cardigan.

eponyms.name: Don Quixote
eponyms.origin: From Don Quixote, the idealistic hero of Miguel de Cervantes’ novel, plus the suffix -ic.

eponyms.name: Étienne de Silhouette
eponyms.origin: From the surname of Étienne de Silhouette (1709–1767), a French finance minister. Why his name was attached to outline portraits is not settled: suggestions include his penny-pinching policies, his short time in office and his own outline portraits.

eponyms.name: Jules Léotard
eponyms.origin: Named after Jules Léotard.

eponyms.name: Joseph-Ignace Guillotin
eponyms.origin: From French guillotine, after Joseph-Ignace Guillotin, who proposed its use for executions.

eponyms.name: Rudolf Diesel
eponyms.origin: After Rudolf Diesel, who developed the engine in Germany in the 1890s.

eponyms.name: Adolphe Sax
eponyms.origin: The surname of its inventor, Adolphe Sax (1814–1894), plus -o- and -phone, from Greek φωνή (phōnḗ) ‘sound, voice’.

eponyms.name: Jean Nicot
eponyms.origin: After Jean Nicot, the French ambassador to Portugal who sent tobacco seeds back to France in 1561, plus the suffix -ine.

eponyms.name: Louis Braille
eponyms.origin: Borrowed from French, after Louis Braille. It names a system of raised dots that is read by touch.

eponyms.name: Franz Anton Mesmer
eponyms.origin: From mesmerism, named after Franz Anton Mesmer (1734–1815), a German physician who developed the theory of ‘animal magnetism’.

eponyms.name: Luigi Galvani
eponyms.origin: After the Italian physiologist Luigi Galvani (1737–1798), by way of galvanism. Its older sense was ‘to electrify’; ‘to shock into action’ grew out of that.

eponyms.name: Louis Pasteur
eponyms.origin: Borrowed from French pasteuriser, from Louis Pasteur, who devised the heating process, plus -ize.

eponyms.name: Amelia Bloomer
eponyms.origin: Named after Amelia Bloomer, who sought to introduce this style of dress for women.

eponyms.name: Ambrose Burnside
eponyms.origin: Reshaped from burnside, after Ambrose Burnside, who was noted for his unusual facial hair.

eponyms.name: Henry Shrapnel
eponyms.origin: After Henry Shrapnel, who invented a shell that scattered bullets over a target.

eponyms.name: Samuel Maverick
eponyms.origin: From Samuel Maverick (1803–1870), who refused to brand his cattle. A maverick was first an unbranded animal, then a person who shows independence in thought or action.

eponyms.name: Nicolas Chauvin
eponyms.origin: Borrowed from French chauvinisme, named after Nicolas Chauvin, a legendary and excessively patriotic soldier made famous by a stage play. He may never have existed.

eponyms.name: Thomas Bowdler
eponyms.origin: After Thomas Bowdler, who in 1818 published The Family Shakespeare, with the words he thought unfit to be read aloud in a family taken out.

eponyms.name: Mrs. Malaprop
eponyms.origin: From Mrs. Malaprop, a character in Richard Brinsley Sheridan’s play The Rivals (1775) who mixes up similar-sounding words. Her name probably comes from French mal à propos ‘inappropriate’.

eponyms.name: Niccolò Machiavelli
eponyms.origin: From Niccolò Machiavelli (1469–1527), whose book The Prince advises that gaining and keeping power may require unethical methods.

eponyms.name: William Archibald Spooner
eponyms.origin: After the Reverend W. A. Spooner of Oxford, who is supposed to have often swapped the sounds of words by mistake.

eponyms.name: Draco
eponyms.origin: After Draco, the Athenian lawmaker known for very harsh laws (his name is the Greek word δράκων, drákōn, ‘dragon’).

eponyms.name: Elbridge Gerry
eponyms.origin: A blend of Gerry and salamander, after Elbridge Gerry, governor of Massachusetts: in 1812 the Boston Gazette compared a district he signed into law to the shape of a salamander.

eponyms.name: George Washington Gale Ferris Jr.
eponyms.origin: After George W. G. Ferris Jr., who built the first such wheel.

eponyms.name: Theodore “Teddy” Roosevelt
eponyms.origin: Made in 1902 by the Brooklyn shop owner Morris Michtom, who named it in honor of President Theodore “Teddy” Roosevelt after hearing that Roosevelt had refused to shoot a bear cub on a hunting trip.

eponyms.name: Joel Roberts Poinsett
eponyms.origin: From an old genus name honoring Joel Roberts Poinsett, the 19th-century US minister to Mexico.

eponyms.name: Anders Dahl
eponyms.origin: Named in 1791 after the Swedish botanist Anders Dahl by the Spanish botanist Antonio José Cavanilles.

eponyms.name: Pierre Magnol
eponyms.origin: From the genus name Magnolia, after the French botanist Pierre Magnol (1638–1715).

eponyms.name: Charles Macintosh
eponyms.origin: From Charles Macintosh (1766–1843), who patented a rubberized cloth in 1823. The k is a later addition to the spelling.

eponyms.name: Lord Raglan
eponyms.origin: Named after Lord Raglan (1788–1855), a British commander in the Crimean War.

eponyms.name: Alessandro Volta
eponyms.origin: The unit is named after Alessandro Volta.

eponyms.name: James Watt
eponyms.origin: The unit is named after James Watt.

eponyms.name: Anders Celsius
eponyms.origin: After Anders Celsius, who proposed the centigrade temperature scale in 1742.

eponyms.name: Daniel Elmer Salmon
eponyms.origin: From the genus name Salmonella, after Daniel Elmer Salmon.

eponyms.name: John Duns Scotus
eponyms.origin: From John Duns Scotus, a well-known medieval Scottish thinker. His later followers opposed the new learning of the Renaissance, so by 1530 dunce meant someone who rejected new knowledge, and later anyone thought stupid.

eponyms.name: Saint Audrey (Æthelthryth)
eponyms.origin: Shortened from tawdry lace, a slurred form of Saint Audrey lace: lace necklaces sold to pilgrims of Saint Audrey. When they went out of fashion, tawdry came to mean ‘cheap and showy’.

eponyms.name: Mary Magdalene
eponyms.origin: From Maudelen, an old form of the name Mary Magdalene, who was usually shown weeping in art.

eponyms.name: Guy Fawkes
eponyms.origin: From Guy Fawkes, executed for his part in the Gunpowder Plot. His effigies, burned every Guy Fawkes Night, were called guys, and the word widened to mean any man.

eponyms.name: Franz Kafka
eponyms.origin: Kafka plus -esque, after the writer Franz Kafka.

eponyms.name: George Orwell
eponyms.origin: From the surname of George Orwell, the pen name of the English writer Eric Arthur Blair (1903–1950).

eponyms.name: Mausolus
eponyms.origin: Through Latin from Greek Μαυσωλεῖον (Mausōleîon), the grand tomb built around 353–351 BCE at Halicarnassus for Mausolus, a ruler of Caria.

eponyms.name: Ceres
eponyms.origin: Through French from Latin Cereālis ‘of Ceres’, the Roman goddess of agriculture.

eponyms.name: Vulcan
eponyms.origin: From Italian vulcano, after the island of Vulcano, named from Latin Vulcānus, the Roman god of fire.

eponyms.name: Atlas
eponyms.origin: From the Titan Atlas of Greek myth, who bore the heavens. Mercator named his book of maps after him, and the sense ‘book of maps’ comes from that.

eponyms.name: Tantalus
eponyms.origin: From Tantalus of Greek myth, condemned to stand in water that drew back when he stooped to drink, under fruit that was always out of reach.

eponyms.name: Pan
eponyms.origin: Through French panique from Greek πανικός (panikós) ‘of Pan’. Pan, the god of fields and woods, was believed to cause sudden groundless fear in herds and crowds.

eponyms.name: Jupiter (Jove)
eponyms.origin: Through French and Italian from Latin Ioviālis ‘of Jupiter’. People born under the astrological influence of the planet Jupiter were believed to be cheerful.

eponyms.name: Odysseus
eponyms.origin: From the Odyssey, the Greek epic telling the long journey home of Odysseus.

eponyms.name: Akademos
eponyms.origin: From Greek Ἀκαδημία (Akadēmía), a grove outside Athens where Plato taught, named after its supposed former owner, the hero Akademos.

eponyms.name: Nîmes, France
eponyms.origin: From French de Nîmes ‘from Nîmes’, the French town where the fabric was first made.

eponyms.name: Genoa, Italy
eponyms.origin: From Gene or Jean, an old English name for Genoa. Jean fustian was a coarse cotton cloth linked with the city; the word was used for trousers of that cloth in the 19th century.

eponyms.name: Tuxedo Park, New York
eponyms.origin: From Tuxedo Park, New York, where the fashion is often said to have started.

eponyms.name: Bikini Atoll
eponyms.origin: From French bikini, after Bikini Atoll, where the United States tested nuclear weapons in July 1946; the swimsuit was expected to cause as much excitement as a bomb.

eponyms.name: Marathon, Greece
eponyms.origin: Coined in French in 1894 by Michel Bréal for the first modern Olympic Games, after the Greek town of Marathon: the legend says Phidippides ran from Marathon to Athens with news of the battle.

eponyms.name: Laconia, Greece
eponyms.origin: Through Latin from Greek Λακωνικός (Lakōnikós) ‘of Laconia’, the region ruled by the Spartans, who were known for speaking briefly.

eponyms.name: Hamburg, Germany
eponyms.origin: Short for Hamburger steak or Hamburger sandwich, from German Hamburger ‘of Hamburg’.

eponyms.name: Cologne, Germany
eponyms.origin: From eau de Cologne ‘water of Cologne’, the name given to the original scent in 1709.

eponyms.name: Corinth, Greece
eponyms.origin: From Anglo-Norman raisin de Corinthe ‘grapes of Corinth’.

eponyms.name: Kocs, Hungary
eponyms.origin: Through French and German from Hungarian kocsi ‘of Kocs’, short for kocsi szekér ‘cart from Kocs’, a small Hungarian town known for its carts. The ‘tutor’ sense began as Oxford University slang around 1830.

eponyms.name: the Maeander river
eponyms.origin: From Latin Maeander, from Greek Μαίανδρος (Maíandros), a river in Asia Minor known for its winding course.

eponyms.name: Bethlem Royal Hospital, London
eponyms.origin: From Bedlam, the popular name of the Bethlem Royal Hospital in London, an asylum (the name is a worn-down form of Bethlehem). It came to mean any scene of uproar.

eponyms.name: the Canary Islands
eponyms.origin: Through French and Spanish from the Canary Islands, Latin Canariae insulae. The largest island was named for its dogs, from Latin canis ‘dog’, so the bird is named, at a distance, after dogs.

eponyms.name: Magnesia
eponyms.origin: Through Latin from Greek μάγνης (mágnēs) ‘magnet, lodestone’, the ‘Magnesian’ stone, named after Magnesia: either the city of Magnesia in Lydia or the Greek region of Magnesia.

eponyms.name: Badminton House, Gloucestershire
eponyms.origin: Named after Badminton House, the Duke of Beaufort’s estate in Gloucestershire, where the game was first played in England.

eponyms.name: Rugby School, Warwickshire
eponyms.origin: From Rugby School in Rugby, Warwickshire, where the modern game was developed in the 19th century.

eponyms.name: Champagne, France
eponyms.origin: From French champagne, the sparkling wine of the Champagne region, whose name comes from Latin campānia, from campus ‘field, plain’.

eponyms.name: Bengal
eponyms.origin: Borrowed from a Gujarati word meaning ‘Bengali-style house’ (compare Hindi baṅglā ‘Bengali’), from the name of Bengal.

eponyms.name: Sweden
eponyms.origin: From French gants de Suède ‘gloves from Sweden’.

eponyms.name: Mosul, Iraq
eponyms.origin: From French mousseline, from Italian mussolina, from Mussolo, the Italian name of Mosul in northern Iraq.

eponyms.name: Calicut (Kozhikode), India
eponyms.origin: From Calicut (Kozhikode), the Indian port from which the cloth was first exported.

words.route: French hôtel, from Old French hostel

doublets.note: All three began as places that take in guests. Hostel fell out of use for over a century until Walter Scott revived it in 1808.

words.route: French fragile, or straight from Latin

doublets.note: Frail was worn down in Old French speech; fragile keeps a spelling much closer to the Latin.
English kept the w-; Old French turned the Germanic w- into gu-. The same split shows in warranty and guarantee, and warden and guardian.
The Norman French used in England kept the w-, while central French had gu-; English borrowed both.
Another w-/gu- pair: the Norman form gave warden, the central French form gave guardian.

words.route: modern French chef, from chef de cuisine

doublets.note: The same French word, borrowed twice: first for a leader, much later for the head of a kitchen.
‘Personal property’, ‘cows’ and ‘money for trade’ all grew from one word for property. Wiktionary links the money sense to medieval trading in head of cattle.
Both go back to a Latin word for a drink; potable is a more distant relative.
Sure is the form that passed through French speech; secure was taken straight from Latin.
Loyal is the form worn down in French; legal came straight from Latin. Leal, an old and Scots word for loyal, is a third relative.

words.route: Old French regal, closer to the Latin

doublets.note: French speech wore rēgālis down to roial; regal keeps the g.
Dainty came through everyday French; dignity kept a shape closer to the Latin.
Old French squeezed the long word down to blasmer; blaspheme kept its religious sense and fuller shape.
Count arrived worn down through French; compute was borrowed again in the 1600s in its Latin shape.
One verb, two shapes: sever through French, separate from the Latin past participle.
Spices were a ‘kind’ of goods; species kept the scientific sense of ‘kind’.
Ratio is a third member of the family, borrowed straight from Latin.
A strait is a narrow, tight passage of water; strict is tight in a figurative sense.

origin.gloss: full of zeal (from Greek ζῆλος, zêlos ‘zeal, jealousy’)

doublets.note: The Greek word already meant both eager devotion and jealousy; English split the senses between two spellings.
A tradition is handed down; treason hands your side over to the enemy.

origin.gloss: disc, quoit, dish (from Greek δίσκος, dískos)

words.route: Medieval Latin desca, from Italian desco

doublets.note: One round, flat object became a plate, a table, a raised platform, a disc and a throwing weight.
A twelfth of a foot and a twelfth of a (Roman) pound: one word, borrowed at two different times.
English softened sk- to sh-; Old Norse kept sk-, and English later borrowed the Norse form too.
Learning was linked with magic, and the Scots form glamour first meant an enchantment before it meant alluring charm.

words.route: Old French cors (the p was put back later)

doublets.note: A dead body, a body of soldiers and a body of texts.
A sergeant was first simply someone who served.
Charter belongs to the same family.
Channel shows the French sound change from ca- to cha-; canal keeps the Latin shape.

words.route: straight from Latin, first as a legal term

doublets.note: Poor came through everyday French; pauper was borrowed later for the law courts.

words.route: Old French parcelle, from Italian particella

doublets.note: A parcel was once a small part of something, as in ‘part and parcel’.
Native came through Old French; naive is the modern French feminine form, with the French spelling.

origin.gloss: label, note (from a Germanic verb ‘to stick’)

doublets.note: One French word for a label or note: ticket came through older French, and etiquette was borrowed again in 1740.
A costume was the customary dress of a place or time.
Both mean to shorten, one through French and one straight from Latin.
A mayor is the ‘greater’ person of a town.
A pungent smell and a poignant memory both sting.
A ransom buys a captive back.

words.route: Anglo-Norman essample, losing its first syllable

doublets.note: Sample is example with the beginning worn away.

words.route: Middle English hole, hool (the wh- spelling appears around 1400)
Middle English hale, a northern form

doublets.note: A doublet inside English itself: two regional forms of the same Old English word.

words.route: Italian zero, from Medieval Latin zephirum

doublets.note: Cipher once meant the figure 0 itself; the Arabic word is a translation of Sanskrit śūnya ‘empty’.

words.route: Ottoman Turkish, Italian turbante, French turbant

doublets.note: Both came west through Ottoman Turkish tülbend.

origin.gloss: a making; a group acting together (from facere)

doublets.note: Fashion is a way of making things; a faction is a group that acts together.
To prosecute a case is to follow it through.

origin.gloss: to try to catch (from capere ‘to take’)

doublets.note: Northern French kept the hard c-; Parisian French turned it into ch-.
To quit is to be set free and at rest; coy first meant quiet and still.

origin.gloss: of the same clan or family (from gēns ‘clan’)

doublets.note: Gentle first meant high-born; genteel and jaunty are later borrowings of the same French gentil.

words.route: Old French humain, an older spelling

doublets.note: Humane was once just another spelling of human. Human became the usual spelling in the early 1700s, and humane kept the sense of kindness.

origin.gloss: person; a mask or character in a play

doublets.note: In Anglo-Norman, persone meant both ‘person’ and ‘parson’.

myths.myth: It is an acronym of “port out, starboard home”, for the shady cabins that wealthy passengers booked on ships between Britain and India.
myths.truth: There is no evidence for the acronym. The origin is not known for certain; the most likely source is Romani posh ‘half’, through slang words for money such as posh-kooroona ‘half a crown’. A slang sense ‘dandy’ from the 1890s may also be related.

myths.myth: It stands for “Gentlemen Only, Ladies Forbidden”.
myths.truth: English took the word in the 17th century from Middle Scots golf, gouff. Its deeper origin is uncertain; the most likely source is Middle Dutch colf, colve ‘club’. Nothing in the word’s recorded history points to an acronym.

myths.myth: It comes from Latin sine cērā ‘without wax’, because honest sculptors did not hide cracks in marble with wax.
myths.truth: It comes from Latin sincērus ‘genuine, pure’; Wiktionary states plainly that it is not from sine + cēra. The deeper history of sincērus is a scholarly reconstruction, not a certainty.

myths.myth: An old law let a man beat his wife with a stick no thicker than his thumb.
myths.truth: The phrase is recorded from 1658 and its origin is uncertain, but it most probably refers to using the thumb as a rough measure. Wiktionary calls the wife-beating claim erroneous and notes that it may come from a 1976 book.

myths.myth: It is an acronym of North, East, West, South (or “Noteworthy Events, Weather, Sports”).
myths.truth: News is simply new used as a noun, Middle English newes, ‘new things’. Wiktionary describes the acronym claims as erroneous.

myths.myth: It stands for “Save Our Souls” or “Save Our Ship”.
myths.truth: It does not stand for anything. The Morse pattern · · · — — — · · · was chosen because it is easy to remember and send; the letters S, O, S are just how that pattern is written.

myths.myth: It was coined from “Old Kinderhook”, Martin Van Buren’s nickname (or from a Choctaw word, okeh).
myths.truth: The origin is disputed. The best-supported account is that OK abbreviates oll korrect, a joke spelling of ‘all correct’, first printed in The Boston Morning Post on 23 March 1839 during a craze for such abbreviations. Van Buren’s 1840 campaign, with his “Old Kinderhook” nickname, helped make it popular. The Choctaw okeh explanation was common in dictionaries until the 1960s but is now less favoured.

myths.myth: It is an acronym of “Constable On Patrol”.
myths.truth: Cop is short for copper ‘police officer’, from the verb cop ‘to seize, catch’, in reference to arresting criminals. Wiktionary calls the acronym an erroneous folk etymology.

myths.myth: It comes from French “Marie malade” (‘Mary is ill’), after the jam given to a sick Mary, Queen of Scots.
myths.truth: It comes through French marmelade from Portuguese marmelada, a quince paste, from marmelo ‘quince’. The Mary story is a false folk etymology.

myths.myth: It comes from Latin sine nobilitate ‘without nobility’, written “s. nob.” next to the names of common students.
myths.truth: Snob was late 18th-century dialect for a shoemaker, of unknown origin. Early uses had no link to the Latin phrase; the modern sense was popularized by Thackeray’s The Book of Snobs (1848).

myths.myth: Napoleon called the dark bread “pain pour Nicole”, fit only for his horse Nicole.
myths.truth: It is a Westphalian German word, from Pumper ‘fart’ and Nickel ‘rascal’ (a form of Nicholas), perhaps first an insult from outsiders. The Napoleon story is a false folk etymology.

myths.myth: Female is male with fe- added in front.
myths.truth: It comes through Old French femelle from Latin fēmella ‘a girl, young woman’, a diminutive of fēmina ‘woman’. Middle English femele was respelled and re-pronounced to match male, which is otherwise unrelated. So the look of the word owes something to male, but its origin does not.

myths.myth: History means “his story”, the story told by and about men.
myths.truth: History comes through Old French and Latin historia from Greek ἱστορία (historía) ‘learning through research, inquiry’. The his- has nothing to do with the pronoun; herstory is a deliberate play on words built on that misreading.

myths.myth: It began as “flutterby” and the sounds were later swapped.
myths.truth: It goes back to Old English buterflēoge, butter + fly. Wiktionary says it was not derived from flutterby. Why butter is not known: the name may first have been used for yellow butterflies, or reflect an old belief that butterflies stole milk and butter.

myths.myth: It refers to the length of a machine-gun ammunition belt, or the cloth in a kilt or a sari.
myths.truth: Research summarized on Wiktionary finds no single origin: it grew from a vague use of yard as an amount, later fixed with whole and a number, and was long a regional American phrase before it spread in the mid-20th century. None of the popular explanations is supported.

myths.myth: Innkeepers kept tallies of pints and quarts, so customers were told to watch their Ps and Qs.
myths.truth: The origin is unknown. Wiktionary, citing the Oxford English Dictionary, calls the pints-and-quarts story a folk etymology and notes that the common ‘mind the letters p and q’ explanation does not fit the earliest uses either.

myths.myth: Workers threw their wooden clogs (sabots) into machines to break them.
myths.truth: Sabotage is from French saboter, from sabot ‘clog’. The clog-throwing story is often told to explain it, but Wiktionary marks it as disputed.
